title: Reaction Mechanisms
lead: Most reactions take place as a sequence of elementary steps, the reaction’s mechanism. The section counts the reactant entities in each step, writes rate laws for single steps, and compares the rate law a proposed mechanism predicts with the one found by experiment, through the step that limits the rate.
objectives: Distinguish net reactions from elementary reactions (steps)
Identify the molecularity of elementary reactions
Write a balanced chemical equation for a process given its reaction mechanism
Derive the rate law consistent with a given reaction mechanism
summary_html: The sequence of individual steps, or elementary reactions, by which reactants are converted into products during the course of a reaction is called the reaction mechanism. The molecularity of an elementary reaction is the number of reactant entities involved, typically one (unimolecular), two (bimolecular), or, less commonly, three (termolecular). The overall rate of a reaction is determined by the rate of the slowest in its mechanism, called the rate-determining step. Unimolecular elementary reactions have first-order rate laws, while bimolecular elementary reactions have second-order rate laws. By comparing the rate laws derived from a reaction mechanism to that determined experimentally, the mechanism may be deemed either incorrect or plausible.

exercises.prompt:
The first step of a proposed multistep mechanism is:
$$\text{F}_{2}(g)\rightleftharpoons 2\text{F}(g)\;\text{fast}$$
Derive the equation relating atomic fluorine concentration to molecular fluorine concentration.
Why are elementary reactions involving three or more reactants very uncommon?

answer.solution: Elementary reactions involving three or more reactants are very uncommon because all the reactant entities must collide at the same instant, and such simultaneous collisions are rare. The probability of three particles colliding simultaneously is less than one one-thousandth of the probability of two particles colliding, so a termolecular step occurs far less often than a bimolecular one under the same conditions. Each additional particle must arrive at that same moment as well, so a collision of four or more particles is less likely still and is practically never observed. A reaction whose equation shows three or more reactants therefore almost always proceeds through a mechanism of unimolecular and bimolecular steps; only a few termolecular steps are established, such as those that appear to be involved in the reaction of nitric oxide with oxygen.

exercises.prompt: In general, can we predict the effect of doubling the concentration of A on the rate of the overall reaction $A+B\;\longrightarrow \;C$? Can we predict the effect if the reaction is known to be an elementary reaction?

answer.solution: No. In general, for the overall reaction, we cannot predict the effect of changing the concentration without knowing the rate law. Yes. If the reaction is an elementary reaction, then doubling the concentration of A doubles the rate.

exercises.prompt:
Define these terms:
(a) unimolecular reaction
(b) bimolecular reaction
(c) elementary reaction
(d) overall reaction

answer.solution:
(a) A unimolecular reaction is an elementary reaction involving a single reactant entity that reacts to produce one or more molecules of product, $A\;\longrightarrow \;\text{products}$, such as ${\text{O}}_{3}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{O}}_{2}+\text{O}$; its rate law is first order, $\krate=\kk\kconcA$.
(b) A bimolecular reaction is an elementary reaction involving two reactant entities, $A+B\;\longrightarrow \;\text{products}$ or $2A\;\longrightarrow \;\text{products}$, such as $\text{O}+{\text{O}}_{3}\;\longrightarrow \;2{\text{O}}_{2}$; its rate law is second order, $\krate=\kk\kconcA\kconcB$ or $\krate=\kk\kconcA^{2}$.
(c) An elementary reaction is a reaction that takes place in a single step, precisely as represented by its equation; each step of a reaction mechanism is an elementary reaction, and its rate law can be written from its molecularity.
(d) An overall reaction is the balanced chemical equation for the net change, obtained by adding the elementary reactions of the mechanism, in which intermediates produced in one step and consumed in a later step cancel; for the two-step decomposition of ozone, it is $2{\text{O}}_{3}(g)\;\longrightarrow \;3{\text{O}}_{2}(g)$.

exercises.prompt: What is the rate law for the elementary termolecular reaction $A+2B\;\longrightarrow \;\text{products?}$ For $3A\;\longrightarrow \;\text{products?}$

Given the following reactions and the corresponding rate laws, in which of the reactions might the elementary reaction and the overall reaction be the same?
(a) $\text{Cl}_{2}+\text{CO}\;\longrightarrow \;\text{Cl}_{2}\text{CO}$, $\text{rate}=k{[\text{Cl}_{2}]}^{3/2}[\text{CO}]$
(b) $\text{PCl}_{3}+\text{Cl}_{2}\;\longrightarrow \;\text{PCl}_{5}$, $\text{rate}=k[\text{PCl}_{3}][\text{Cl}_{2}]$
(c) $2\text{NO}+\text{H}_{2}\;\longrightarrow \;\text{N}_{2}+\text{H}_{2}\text{O}_{2}$, $\text{rate}=k[\text{NO}][\text{H}_{2}]$
(d) $2\text{NO}+\text{O}_{2}\;\longrightarrow \;2\text{NO}_{2}$, $\text{rate}=k{[\text{NO}]}^{2}[\text{O}_{2}]$
(e) $\text{NO}+\text{O}_{3}\;\longrightarrow \;\text{NO}_{2}+\text{O}_{2}$, $\text{rate}=k[\text{NO}][\text{O}_{3}]$

answer.solution: Reactions (b), (d) and (e) might be single elementary reactions, and reactions (a) and (c) cannot be. If a reaction were one elementary step, its rate law would follow from its equation, each concentration raised to the power of that reactant’s coefficient. For (a), that would be $\text{rate}=k[\text{Cl}_{2}][\text{CO}]$, but the observed rate law has ${[\text{Cl}_{2}]}^{3/2}$, a fractional order no single step can give. For (b), the predicted $\text{rate}=k[\text{PCl}_{3}][\text{Cl}_{2}]$ matches the given rate law. For (c), the predicted $\text{rate}=k{[\text{NO}]}^{2}[\text{H}_{2}]$ differs from the given first order in NO. For (d), the predicted $\text{rate}=k{[\text{NO}]}^{2}[\text{O}_{2}]$ matches, consistent with the termolecular step this reaction appears to involve. For (e), the predicted $\text{rate}=k[\text{NO}][\text{O}_{3}]$ matches. A matching rate law shows only that a single step is possible, not that it is the actual mechanism.

exercises.prompt:
Write the rate law for each of the following elementary reactions:
(a) $\text{O}_{3}\overset{\;\text{sunlight}\;}{\to}\text{O}_{2}+\text{O}$
(b) $\text{O}_{3}+\text{Cl}\;\longrightarrow \;\text{O}_{2}+\text{ClO}$
(c) $\text{ClO}+\text{O}\;\longrightarrow \;\text{Cl}+\text{O}_{2}$
(d) $\text{O}_{3}+\text{NO}\;\longrightarrow \;\text{NO}_{2}+\text{O}_{2}$
(e) $\text{NO}_{2}+\text{O}\;\longrightarrow \;\text{NO}+\text{O}_{2}$

Nitrogen monoxide, NO, reacts with hydrogen, H<sub>2</sub>, according to the following equation:
$$2\text{NO}+2\text{H}_{2}\;\longrightarrow \;\text{N}_{2}+2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$
What would the rate law be if the mechanism for this reaction were:
$$\begin{array}{l}2\text{NO}+\text{H}_{2}\;\longrightarrow \;\text{N}_{2}+\text{H}_{2}\text{O}_{2}\;(\text{slow}) \\ \text{H}_{2}\text{O}_{2}+\text{H}_{2}\;\longrightarrow \;2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}\;(\text{fast})\end{array}$$

answer.solution: $\text{rate}=k{[\text{NO}]}^{2}[\text{H}_{2}]$. The first step is the slow one, so it is the rate-determining step, and when the first step is the slow one, the rate law for the overall reaction is the rate law of that step. As an elementary reaction, $2\text{NO}+\text{H}_{2}\;\longrightarrow \;\text{N}_{2}+\text{H}_{2}\text{O}_{2}$ has a rate law written from its molecularity: second order in NO, from its coefficient of 2, and first order in H<sub>2</sub>, third order overall. The fast second step consumes the H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> as fast as it forms and does not affect the rate. The mechanism is consistent with the equation, because adding the two steps cancels the intermediate H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> and gives $2\text{NO}+2\text{H}_{2}\;\longrightarrow \;\text{N}_{2}+2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.

parts.hint: Find the orders by comparing experiments that change one concentration at a time, then solve the rate law for k with the numbers of any one experiment.
The equation uses NO and H<sub>2</sub> in a 2:2 ratio, so each mole of H<sub>2</sub> consumed uses one mole of NO.

answer.solution: (a) Doubling [H2] doubles the rate. [H2] must enter the rate law to the first power. Doubling [NO] increases the rate by a factor of 4. [NO] must enter the rate law to the second power. (b) Rate = k [NO]2[H2]; (c) k = 5.0 × 103 mol2 L−2 min−1; (d) 0.0050 mol/L; (e) Step II is the rate-determining step. If step I gives N2O2 in adequate amount, steps 1 and 2 combine to give $2\text{NO}+\text{H}_{2}\;\longrightarrow \;\text{H}_{2}\text{O}+\text{N}_{2}\text{O}.$ This reaction corresponds to the observed rate law. Combine steps 1 and 2 with step 3, which occurs by supposition in a rapid fashion, to give the appropriate stoichiometry.

exercises.prompt:
The reaction of CO with Cl2 gives phosgene (COCl2), a poisonous gas used as a chemical weapon during World War I. Use the mechanism shown here to complete the following exercises:
$\text{Cl}_{2}(g)\;\rightleftharpoons \;2\text{Cl}(g)$ (fast, k1 represents the forward rate constant, k−1 the reverse rate constant)
$\text{CO}(g)+\text{Cl}(g)\;\longrightarrow \;\text{COCl}(g)$ (slow, k2 the rate constant)
$\text{COCl}(g)+\text{Cl}(g)\;\longrightarrow \;\text{COCl}_{2}(g)$ (fast, k3 the rate constant)
(a) Write the overall reaction.
(b) Identify all intermediates.
(c) Write the rate law for each elementary reaction.
(d) Write the overall rate law expression.

answer.solution:
(a) $\text{CO}(g)+\text{Cl}_{2}(g)\;\longrightarrow \;\text{COCl}_{2}(g)$. Adding the three steps gives $\text{Cl}_{2}+\text{CO}+\text{Cl}+\text{COCl}+\text{Cl}\;\longrightarrow \;2\text{Cl}+\text{COCl}+\text{COCl}_{2}$, and the two Cl atoms and the COCl cancel from both sides.
(b) Cl and COCl are the intermediates: Cl is produced in the first step and consumed in the second and third, and COCl is produced in the second step and consumed in the third.
(c) Step 1 forward, ${\krate}_{1}=\kkone[\text{Cl}_{2}]$; step 1 reverse, ${\krate}_{-1}=\kkmone{[\text{Cl}]}^{2}$; step 2, ${\krate}_{2}=\kktwo[\text{CO}][\text{Cl}]$; step 3, ${\krate}_{3}={\kk}_{3}[\text{COCl}][\text{Cl}]$.
(d) $\krate=\kktwo{\left(\frac{\kkone}{\kkmone}\right)}^{1/2}[\text{CO}]{[\text{Cl}_{2}]}^{1/2}$, or $\krate=\kk[\text{CO}]{[\text{Cl}_{2}]}^{1/2}$. The slow second step determines the rate, $\krate=\kktwo[\text{CO}][\text{Cl}]$, but [Cl] is the concentration of an intermediate. The fast first step is at equilibrium, so its forward and reverse rates are equal, $\kkone[\text{Cl}_{2}]=\kkmone{[\text{Cl}]}^{2}$, which gives $[\text{Cl}]={\left(\frac{\kkone}{\kkmone}\right)}^{1/2}{[\text{Cl}_{2}]}^{1/2}$. Substituting this into the rate law of step 2 gives the overall rate law, with $\kk=\kktwo{\left(\frac{\kkone}{\kkmone}\right)}^{1/2}$.
